nodes.label: Foundation of Trebizond
nodes.full: The brothers Alexios and David Komnenos, grandsons of Andronikos I, took Trebizond in April 1204 with Georgian help from their kinswoman Queen Tamar, a few days before the Crusaders took Constantinople. Alexios was proclaimed emperor, while David seized the Black Sea coast as far as Heraclea, so that they held a Pontic empire. It shrank to the coast of Pontus.
nodes.src: Michael Panaretos; George Akropolites; Anthony Bryer, The Empire of Trebizond and the Pontos (1980); William Miller, Trebizond: The Last Greek Empire (1926).

nodes.label: The empire of the East
nodes.full: After the Fourth Crusade, Trebizond claimed with Nicaea and Epirus the succession of the Byzantine emperors, and its rulers called themselves Emperor of the Romans. The claim could not be enforced, but it gave the Pontic Greeks an imperial identity that lasted after 1461.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Fall of Sinope
nodes.full: Kaykaus I, sultan of Rum, took Sinope, the empire's western port, in 1214, and captured Alexios I, who was released as a vassal. Trebizond lost the coast to the west of Sinope and its way into Paphlagonia. It had to pay tribute to the sultan for the next 30 years.
nodes.src: Ibn Bibi; Panaretos; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Manuel I and predecessors
nodes.full: After Alexios's death the sons-in-law Andronikos I Gidos and John I Axouchos held the throne in succession, and Manuel I, 'the Great Captain', ruled for 25 years. He paid tribute to the Seljuks of Rum and, after 1243, to the Mongols. In his time the Hagia Sophia of Trebizond was built and the city became a centre of the trade between Persia and the Black Sea.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Ibn Bibi; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Mongol overlordship
nodes.full: After the Köse Dağ the emperors of Trebizond paid tribute to the Mongol governors of Anatolia, and later to the Ilkhans, and sent daughters and gifts. The Mongol overlordship brought the Persian trade to the city and protected it from the Turkmen.
nodes.src: Ibn Bibi; Panaretos; Bryer 1980; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Hagia Sophia of Trebizond
nodes.full: Built under Manuel I on a hillside by the sea, in a mixture of the Byzantine cross-in-square plan and Seljuk-style stonework, the church of Hagia Sophia has a portal with a carved frieze of Adam and Eve and animals, and on its walls and in its narthex a wide cycle of 13th-century wall paintings. It is the most important monument of the empire.
nodes.src: David Talbot Rice (ed.), The Church of Haghia Sophia at Trebizond (1968); Bryer and Winfield 1985.

nodes.label: John II and the title of the East
nodes.full: John II married Eudokia, the daughter of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, in 1282 and gave up the title Emperor of the Romans, which his predecessors had borne, for Emperor and Autocrat of All the East, the Iberians and the Transmarine Lands. He kept the throne and the independence of Trebizond and made peace with Constantinople.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Pachymeres; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Alexios II
nodes.full: Alexios II, John II's son, ruled for 33 years, in a time of wealth for Trebizond with the Ilkhanid trade, and in 1319 granted Venice a trade treaty. His reign was troubled by the quarrels with the Genoese at Leontokastron and by the raids of Turkmen groups from the hills. He was succeeded by a sequence of short, violent reigns.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Bryer 1980; Venetian chrysobull of 1319 (Tafel and Thomas).

nodes.label: Venetian chrysobull
nodes.full: Alexios II granted the Venetians a quarter and exemption from customs in the city, with the right to maintain a church, a bailo and a court under their own law. The treaty gave Venice a counterweight to the Genoese and secured a place on the route to Tabriz.
nodes.src: Chrysobull of Alexios II to Venice (Tafel and Thomas, Urkunden 1856–57); Balard 1978.

nodes.label: Genoese Leontokastron
nodes.full: The Genoese, who were allowed a quarter outside the city in the later thirteenth century, fortified it at Leontokastron from 1306, which led to conflicts with the emperors and a series of attacks by both sides. It was the centre of Genoa's trade with Persia for most of the century.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Michel Balard, La Romanie génoise (1978); Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Court of the Grand Komnenoi
nodes.full: The court of Trebizond modelled itself on Constantinople: with a Great Palace, the offices of the Byzantine bureaucracy, the titles of the aristocracy and the ceremonial of Byzantine emperors, with some oriental features such as a Persian tradition of the hunt. The emperor was the Grand Komnenos. The resemblance was a matter of pride.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Pseudo-Kodinos (c. 1350); Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: End of the Tabriz road
nodes.full: Trebizond was the Black Sea port at the end of the caravan route over the Zigana pass from Tabriz, which brought silk, spices and pearls of the East, and in return took cloth and metalwork. Marco Polo and Pegolotti mention it, and Genoese, Venetian and Persian merchants lived in the city. The Ilkhanate's trade made it rich.
nodes.src: Marco Polo, Travels 1; Pegolotti, Pratica della mercatura; Balard 1978.

nodes.label: Silver and the asper
nodes.full: The silver mines of Argyroupolis in the hills south of Trebizond gave the empire a source of bullion and a coinage, the asper, which was struck from the early thirteenth century and circulated as a trade silver coin in the Black Sea and Persia. The state's wealth in silver was a factor in the survival of the empire.
nodes.src: Bryer and Winfield 1985; Michael Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985); Panaretos.

nodes.label: Slave trade
nodes.full: Genoese notarial records show the sale of slaves at Trebizond — Circassians, Abkhaz, Georgians, Laz and Tatars — who were shipped to Cairo and Italy. The empire collected tolls on the trade. The Black Sea slave trade was one of the great moving forces of the Mediterranean in the later Middle Ages.
nodes.src: Genoese notarial acts (Balard 1978); Michel Balard, 'Les Génois en mer Noire'; Charles Verlinden, L'esclavage dans l'Europe médiévale vol. 2 (1977).

nodes.label: Chioniades and Persian astronomy
nodes.full: Gregory Chioniades, a Greek physician who went to Tabriz around 1295 and studied astronomy under the Ilkhanid scholars of Maragha, brought Persian planetary tables and models to Trebizond and then Constantinople, and translated them into Greek as the Persian Syntaxis. In the 1340s George Chrysokokkes revised the work. It is a channel by which Islamic astronomy reached the Greek world and later Italy.
nodes.src: Gregory Chioniades, Persian Syntaxis; George Chrysokokkes, Persian Syntaxis (c. 1347); David Pingree, The Astronomical Works of Gregory Chioniades (1985).

nodes.label: Panaretos
nodes.full: Michael Panaretos, an official of the court who served as secretary and protovestiarios, wrote a very short chronicle of the Grand Komnenoi from 1204 to 1390 in plain annalistic form, with dates for each event. It is the main source for the empire's history, of births, marriages, plagues and revolts.
nodes.src: Michael Panaretos, Peri ton Megalon Komnenon (ed. Lampsides, 1958).

nodes.label: Anarchy of the 1340s
nodes.full: After the death of Basil in 1340, six rulers followed each other in nine years: the empresses Irene Palaiologina and Anna Anachoutlou, John III, Michael and others, with noble factions in the city and Turkmen and Genoese bargaining. Alexios III, aged eleven, took the throne in 1349.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Anna Anachoutlou
nodes.full: Anna, a daughter of Alexios II, took the throne in 1341 after the fall of Irene Palaiologina, with the support of a part of the aristocracy, and ruled for about eight months as empress in her own right. She was deposed by a coup and killed on the order of her successor.
nodes.src: Panaretos s.a. 1341; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Black Death
nodes.full: The plague came to Trebizond by sea from the Crimea in 1347, as at Constantinople and the other Black Sea ports, killing much of the population. The city's decline coincided with the plague and the political crisis of the 1340s.
nodes.src: Panaretos s.a. 1347; Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977).

nodes.label: Alexios III
nodes.full: Alexios III took the throne at eleven after the dynastic anarchy of the 1340s and ruled for 41 years. His reign was the empire's peak: the monasteries were enriched, a stream of Turkmen princes married his daughters, the Genoese were held in check and the court produced art and learning. He is the best-documented of the Grand Komnenoi.
nodes.src: Panaretos (to 1390); Bryer 1980; Janin, Les églises et les monastères.

nodes.label: Chrysobulls for monasteries
nodes.full: Emperors from Manuel I to David issued chrysobulls granting lands, villages and revenue to monasteries — Soumela, Vazelon and St. Eugenios of Trebizond and, on Athos, Dionysiou, which Alexios III endowed. The documents record the countryside and the working of the empire's estates, and show the monastic wealth of Pontus.
nodes.src: Chrysobulls of Alexios III for Dionysiou (1374) and Soumela; Janin; Bryer and Winfield, The Byzantine Monuments of the Pontos (1985).

nodes.label: Soumela
nodes.full: The monastery of the Virgin of Soumela, cut into a cliff face 1,200 metres up in the Pontic Alps and said to date from the fourth century, was endowed by Alexios III and rebuilt, with frescoes of the 14th–15th centuries. It was the great pilgrimage site of the Pontic Greeks until the population exchange of 1923.
nodes.src: Soumela chrysobulls; Bryer and Winfield 1985; Rustam Shukurov on Pontic monasteries.

nodes.label: Marriages with Turkmen
nodes.full: The emperors married their daughters to the Turkmen chiefs on the borders — the emirs of Bayburt, Çepni lords and the Ak Koyunlu — to buy peace, in a practice that made Trebizond's princesses the mothers of Turkmen dynasties. The empire's last great marriage was that of John IV's daughter Despina to Uzun Hasan in 1458.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Chalkokondyles; Bryer 1980; Woods 1976.

nodes.label: Turkmen raids
nodes.full: Turkmen groups from the hinterland — the Çepni of the mountains and the Ak Koyunlu and Kara Koyunlu confederations on the eastern plateau — raided the coastal plains and drove Trebizond to accommodate its neighbours with tribute and marriage ties.
nodes.src: Panaretos; Chalkokondyles; Bryer 1980; John Woods, The Aqquyunlu (1976).

nodes.label: Turkmen of the Pontic hills
nodes.full: Turkmen tribes, among them the Çepni, moved into the Pontic mountains in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and by the later fifteenth century they dominated the highlands behind Trebizond. The Greek and Laz coast kept its language and religion, so that a Greek-speaking Christian population survived on the coast.
nodes.src: Bryer 1980; Chalkokondyles; Ottoman tahrir registers of 1486.

nodes.label: Clavijo
nodes.full: The Castilian ambassador Ruy González de Clavijo, on his way to the court of Timur, spent weeks in Trebizond in 1403–1404 and described its harbour, its churches, the Genoese and Venetian quarters and the imperial court. His narrative is a vivid account of the empire in its age of prosperity.
nodes.src: Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane (trans. Guy Le Strange, 1928).

nodes.label: Manuel III to John IV
nodes.full: Manuel III, Alexios IV and John IV Kaloioannes ruled in the age of Timur and the Ottoman advance, and sought help from the Ak Koyunlu, from Georgia and from the West. Their wives and daughters were married to Turkmen chiefs and Byzantine and Georgian princes. By John IV's time, Trebizond was a small state surviving on diplomacy and its old fame.
nodes.src: Laonikos Chalkokondyles; Bessarion, Encomium; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: Bessarion at Florence
nodes.full: Basil Bessarion, born at Trebizond and archbishop of Nicaea, took part in the council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438 and 1439 as one of the leaders of the Greek delegation who believed that union with Rome was the only way to save Byzantium. He signed the decree of union, stayed in Italy and became a cardinal. Trebizond had its first great man in the West.
nodes.src: Council of Florence acts; Bessarion, Orations; Lotte Labowsky, Bessarion's Library (1979).

nodes.label: Bessarion’s Encomium
nodes.full: Bessarion wrote the Encomium of Trebizond in 1436, a rhetorical praise of the city of his birth in the antique style, with details of its site, walls and customs. It shows a literary patriotism in a small empire, and was used by later historians for its descriptions of the city.
nodes.src: Bessarion, Encomium of Trebizond (ed. Lampsides, 1984).

nodes.label: Despina Khatun
nodes.full: Theodora (Despina) Megale Komnene, daughter of John IV, married Uzun Hasan in 1458, and she was the mother of a Ak Koyunlu line. She kept her Christian faith and a Greek retinue at the Turkmen court and used her influence in favour of her relatives, and Christian visitors such as Venetian envoys relied on her.
nodes.src: Ambrogio Contarini, Travels; Josafa Barbaro, Travels; Woods 1976.

nodes.label: David
nodes.full: David, John IV's brother, succeeded in 1459, and counted on the support of Uzun Hasan, Georgia and the pope, with a scheme of an anti-Turkish league, to resist Mehmed II. When the Ottoman army and fleet arrived in the summer of 1461, he surrendered the city and was sent to Constantinople.
nodes.src: Kritovoulos, History 4; Laonikos Chalkokondyles 9; Doukas.

nodes.label: Fall of Trebizond
nodes.full: Mehmed II, after taking Sinope and the Pontic coast and forcing Uzun Hasan to withdraw, came to Trebizond by land and sea in the summer of 1461. After a month's siege the emperor David surrendered the city on terms that left his family and the people safe. The Empire of Trebizond ended, eight years after Constantinople.
nodes.src: Kritovoulos 4; Chalkokondyles 9; Doukas 45; Bryer 1980; Miller 1926.

nodes.label: Last Greek state
nodes.full: After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 Trebizond, with its rump of Greeks and Georgian allies, held out for eight years under the shadow of the Ottomans, who in 1456 made it pay a tribute. It was the last independent Greek state of the Middle Ages.
nodes.src: Chalkokondyles; Kritovoulos 4; Bryer 1980.

nodes.label: David executed
nodes.full: David, last emperor of Trebizond, was given estates in Thrace with his family, and in 1463 Mehmed II, after he was accused of having corresponded with Uzun Hasan, had him and his sons executed, and his niece taken for his harem. The line of the Grand Komnenoi ended in this way.
nodes.src: Kritovoulos 5; Chalkokondyles 9; Doukas; Miller 1926.

nodes.label: Ravine city
nodes.full: The citadel of Trebizond stands on a table of rock between two deep ravines, which formed natural moats, with walls above the sea and a harbour on each side. Its defences held against Turkmen and Genoese for two and a half centuries and were taken only by the Ottomans' combined land and sea attack. The site made a small state defensible.
nodes.src: Bryer and Winfield 1985; Miller 1926.

nodes.label: The Fourth Crusade and the fall of Constantinople
nodes.full: The Crusaders and Venetians took Constantinople in April 1204 and broke up the Byzantine state into successor states, among them those of Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond.
nodes.src: background — see the Seljuks of Rum 1071–1308 folio (seljuks-of-rum-1071-1308), entry w2

nodes.label: The fall of Constantinople
nodes.full: Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453 and ended the Byzantine Empire, leaving Trebizond as the last Greek state.
nodes.src: background — see the Anatolian Beyliks folio (anatolian-beyliks-1308-1500, to be built) and the Byzantine system folios (parked)
